About the "white paper"

Apache does not currently appear to designate a document specifically as "the Apache Tika white paper." The closest authoritative technical/project document is the original Apache Tika project proposal, titled Tika, a content analysis toolkit. Java: 17 or later

Tika can detect and extract text and metadata from over a thousand file types, according to the project documentation. Apache Tika

For example:

Java
import org.apache.tika.Tika;

import java.io.File;

public class DocumentReader {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        Tika tika = new Tika();

        String text =
            tika.parseToString(
                new File("document.pdf")
            );

        System.out.println(text);
    }
}

 of machine learning..."

4. First program: extract its text with Tika

Create:

src\main\java\com\example\CreateOntology.java

Put this code inside:

Java
package com.example;

import org.apache.tika.exception.TikaException;
import org.apache.tika.io.TikaInputStream;
import org.apache.tika.metadata.Metadata;
import org.apache.tika.metadata.TikaCoreProperties;
import org.apache.tika.parser.AutoDetectParser;
import org.apache.tika.parser.ParseContext;
import org.apache.tika.sax.BodyContentHandler;

import java.nio.file.Path;

public class CreateOntology {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        Path document =
                Path.of("documents/machine-learning.pdf");

        Metadata metadata = new Metadata();

        String text;

        try (TikaInputStream stream =
                     TikaInputStream.get(document, metadata)) {

            AutoDetectParser parser =
                    new AutoDetectParser();

            BodyContentHandler handler =
                    new BodyContentHandler(-1);

            ParseContext context =
                    new ParseContext();

            parser.parse(
                    stream,
                    handler,
                    metadata,
                    context
            );

            text = handler.toString();
        }

        System.out.println("TITLE:");
        System.out.println(
                metadata.get(TikaCoreProperties.TITLE)
        );

        System.out.println("\nTEXT:");
        System.out.println(text);
    }
}

This follows Tika's documented AutoDetectParser → BodyContentHandler → Metadata pattern. BodyContentHandler(-1) removes the default 100,000-character output limit, which is useful during this local experiment. Apache Tika

Run it:

PowerShell
mvn clean compile exec:java "-Dexec.mainClass=com.example.CreateOntology"

You should see something like:

TITLE:
Machine Learning Introduction

TEXT:

Artificial intelligence is a field of computer science.

Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence.

Deep learning is a type of machine learning.

Convolutional neural networks are used for image recognition.

Stop here and make sure this works first.

If it does, Tika is successfully reading your real document.

ChatGPT said:

Yes — you can build the entire document → ontology → semantic search pipeline offline.

The parts we discussed can all run locally:

PDF / DOCX / TXT
       ↓
Apache Tika
       ↓
Extracted text
       ↓
Local NLP / Local LLM
       ↓
Classes + relationships
       ↓
Apache Jena
       ↓
OWL / RDF ontology
       ↓
TDB2 / Lucene
       ↓
SPARQL semantic search

Apache Tika works offline for document parsing, Apache Jena works offline for RDF/OWL/SPARQL/inference/storage, and Lucene works offline for text indexing/search. The only part that changes is automatic ontology extraction. If you use something like the OpenAI API, Gemini, Claude, etc., that requires Internet access. If you instead run an NLP model or LLM locally, the whole pipeline can stay offline.

A practical fully offline setup would be:

  • Java 21 for your application, Jena, and Tika.

  • Apache Tika for extracting text and metadata.

  • Local LLM/NLP model for identifying classes, properties, relationships, and hierarchies.

  • Apache Jena 6.2.0 OntAPI for generating OWL/RDF.

  • Jena TDB2 for persistent RDF storage.

  • Lucene / jena-text for local full-text search.

  • Optional Tesseract OCR for scanned PDFs/images.

For example, instead of:

Tika
 ↓
text
 ↓
OpenAI API
 ↓
ontology JSON

you'd use:

Tika
 ↓
text
 ↓
Local model running on your PC
 ↓
ontology JSON

Then Jena handles the rest:

{
  "classes": [
    "MachineLearning",
    "DeepLearning"
  ],
  "subclassOf": [
    {
      "child": "DeepLearning",
      "parent": "MachineLearning"
    }
  ]
}

becomes:

turtle
ex:MachineLearning
    a owl:Class .

ex:DeepLearning
    a owl:Class ;
    rdfs:subClassOf ex:MachineLearning .

There is one catch: the first setup may require Internet access to download Maven dependencies and any local AI model files. Once those dependencies and model weights are already on your machine, you can disconnect from the Internet and run the pipeline locally.

So the offline architecture I would recommend for your project is:

             Your computer
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                      │
│ Documents                            │
│    ↓                                 │
│ Apache Tika                          │
│    ↓                                 │
│ Extracted text                       │
│    ↓                                 │
│ Local LLM / NLP                      │
│    ↓                                 │

│    ↓                                 │
│ Validation / normalization           │
│    ↓                                 │
│ Apache Jena OntAPI                   │

│ TDB2 + Lucene + SPARQL               │
│                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘

           No Internet required

And yes, that means your original goal—automatically creating an ontology from private documents without uploading those documents anywhere—is completely feasible.

3. Call the local model from Java

Ollama normally exposes a local HTTP API.

Your Java application can call:

http://localhost:11434/api/generate

For example:

Java
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient();

String prompt = """
Extract an ontology from this document.

Return only JSON with:
classes,
subclassOf,
properties.

Document:
%s
""".formatted(text);

String body = """
{
  "model": "llama3.1:8b",
  "prompt": %s,
  "stream": false
}
""".formatted(
        new ObjectMapper().writeValueAsString(prompt)
);

HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
        .uri(URI.create(
            "http://localhost:11434/api/generate"
        ))
        .header(
            "Content-Type",
            "application/json"
        )
        .POST(
            HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)
        )
        .build();

HttpResponse<String> response =
        client.send(
            request,
            HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        );

System.out.println(response.body());

So now:

Tika text
   ↓
Java HTTP request
   ↓
Local LLM
   ↓
Ontology JSON

4. Parse the JSON

Add Jackson:

XML
<dependency>

Then define Java objects such as:

Java
class OntologyResult {
    public List<String> classes;
    public List<SubclassRelation> subclassOf;
    public List<PropertyRelation> properties;
}
Java
class SubclassRelation {
    public String child;
    public String parent;
}
Java

    public String range;

Then:

ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();

5. Let Jena create classes automatically

Instead of manually writing:

Java
model.createOntClass(
    NS + "MachineLearning"
);

loop through the extracted classes:

Java
Map<String, OntClass.Named> classes =
        new HashMap<>();

for (String className : result.classes) {

    OntClass.Named ontClass =
            model.createOntClass(
                    NS + className
            );

    classes.put(
            className,
            ontClass
    );
}

Now your ontology classes come from the document automatically.

6. Create subclass relationships automatically

Java
for (SubclassRelation relation :
        result.subclassOf) {

    OntClass.Named child =
            classes.get(relation.child);

    OntClass.Named parent =
            classes.get(relation.parent);

    if (child != null && parent != null) {
        child.addSuperClass(parent);
    }
}

So this JSON:

JSON
{
  "child": "DeepLearning",
  "parent": "MachineLearning"
}

automatically becomes:

turtle
ex:DeepLearning
    rdfs:subClassOf
        ex:MachineLearning .

7. Create properties automatically

Java
for (PropertyRelation relation :
        result.properties) {

    OntObjectProperty.Named property =
            model.createObjectProperty(
                    NS + relation.name
            );

    OntClass.Named domain =
            classes.get(relation.domain);

    OntClass.Named range =
            classes.get(relation.range);

    if (domain != null) {
        property.addDomain(domain);
    }

    if (range != null) {
        property.addRange(range);
    }
}

Now:

JSON
{
  "name": "usedFor",
  "domain": "ConvolutionalNeuralNetwork",
  "range": "ImageRecognition"
}

becomes:

turtle
ex:usedFor
    a owl:ObjectProperty ;
    rdfs:domain
        ex:ConvolutionalNeuralNetwork ;
    rdfs:range
        ex:ImageRecognition .

Same as before:

Java
try (FileOutputStream out =
        new FileOutputStream(
            "output/ontology.ttl"
        )) {

    RDFDataMgr.write(
        out,
        model,
        Lang.TURTLE
    );
}

At that point your pipeline becomes genuinely automatic:

machine-learning.pdf
        ↓
      Tika
        ↓
"Deep learning is a type..."
        ↓
   Local LLM
        ↓
     JSON
        ↓
      Jena
        ↓
output/ontology.ttl

That is the next milestone I would build. Don't add TDB2, Fuseki, Lucene, or semantic search yet. First get one PDF → automatically generated ontology.ttl working reliably.
